claims.text: The target materials are as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA nanoscale thin films or patterned nanoribbons.
The as-deposited films or nanoribbons have high internal microstrain.
The as-deposited films or nanoribbons have small grains and a defect-rich structure.
The as-deposited films or nanoribbons contain nanoscale compositional fluctuations.
Internal stress, defects, and compositional heterogeneity produce spatially variable magnetic exchange interactions.
Spatially variable magnetic exchange and microstructural defects enhance magnetic-domain-wall pinning.
Enhanced domain-wall pinning broadens and diminishes the magnetocaloric entropy-change profile.
Enhanced domain-wall pinning increases magnetic hysteresis during low-field cooling cycles.
The peak magnitude and shape of the entropy-change curve are relevant measures of magnetocaloric refrigeration performance.
Annealing at approximately 400–500 °C in an inert atmosphere will relieve residual stress and reduce defect density.
The proposed annealing treatment will improve compositional homogeneity.
The proposed annealing treatment will increase effective grain size.
Annealing at 400–500 °C can produce stress relief without significant grain growth or phase separation.
Reduced residual stress and defect density will reduce domain-wall pinning and enable more coherent magnetic switching.
Annealing will produce tighter magneto-structural coupling.
Relative to the as-deposited control, annealed samples will have a higher peak magnetocaloric entropy change.
Relative to the as-deposited control, annealed samples will have lower hysteresis and a sharper cooling-transition profile.
A magnetic transition in a nanoscale high-entropy film can be observed under a low applied field near 100 Oe.
Heat-transfer capability limits the usable cooling-cycle frequency in the proposed nanoscale geometry.
Existing evidence supports a general trend of improved magnetocaloric performance and reduced hysteresis after annealing.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as avoiding significant grain growth, while increased effective grain size is listed as a principal annealing-induced mediator. These can coexist only if the intended increase is explicitly defined as small or sub-significant.
